title: Anderson, Policy Committee Highlight Neighbors Helping Neighbors as Families Face Rising Costs
raw_text:
Anderson, Policy Committee Highlight Neighbors Helping Neighbors as Families Face Rising Costs
October 5, 2026
DILLSBURG—The House Republican Policy Committee, chaired by Rep. David H. Rowe (R-Snyder, Union, Mifflin, Juniata), joined Rep. Marc Anderson (R-York) for an Oct. 1 hearing at New Hope Ministries to examine how community organizations are helping Pennsylvania families manage rising costs and how state government can remove barriers that stand in the way of serving their neighbors.
The hearing, “Neighbors Helping Neighbors,” brought together local nonprofit leaders, pastors, veterans advocates, and people who have received assistance. Testimony highlighted food assistance, affordable childcare, housing needs, and the partnerships that help families through difficult times.
In his opening remarks, Rowe cited
United Way of Pennsylvania’s 2026 ALICE report
, which found that nearly four in 10 Pennsylvania households lacked enough income to cover basic needs in 2024, including many earning above the federal poverty level.
“The people who are here today, and so many in northern York County, are skipping the middleman and they're helping people with their own time, their own money, their own resources, and that's what today is about,” Anderson said.
Eric Saunders, executive director of New Hope Ministries, described the organization’s work across York, Adams, and Cumberland counties, including food, housing, employment, and transportation assistance. He testified that governmental support accounts for less than 10% of its annual operating budget and that 2,500 volunteers contributed 150,000 hours of service during the past year.
“We're serving double the number of people and providing more than double the number of services we were just five years ago. Part of that is an affordability crisis,” Saunders said.
Pastor Thad Sales of Calvary Methodist Church described requests for help with rent, utilities, gasoline and prescriptions. The church provides financial assistance, clothing and community meals, while partnering with other local organizations.
“While there are so many wonderful neighbors helping neighbors, it can only go so far. The scale and the scope of rising costs is growing beyond what neighbors can do,” Sales said.
“When we talk about affordability and rising costs, we are talking about decisions that every family makes around their kitchen tables. Can we cover the groceries? How about the electric bill? How much is left after rent? What happens if the car breaks down or somebody has to take a week off work?” Rowe said. “For families already stretching every paycheck, an unexpected expense can put basic necessities out of reach.”
Members also heard from Rodney Carberry, commander of Dillsburg American Legion Post 26, about the post’s support for veterans, schools, local charities, and families. Carberry urged lawmakers to update gaming policies so community organizations can continue raising money to support their charitable work.
Pastor Matthew Castillo, founder of Believers Early Learning Center in York Haven, described families who earn too much to qualify for childcare subsidies but cannot afford full tuition. He asked members to consider ways newly licensed centers could access scholarship support while working toward additional program qualifications.
“But there needs to be some sort of window for new programs to be able to receive these dollars, especially in cases where you're in a childcare desert where it drastically affects the community,” Castillo said.
His testimony prompted discussion of barriers to Educational Improvement Tax Credit (EITC)-supported preschool scholarships and the broader demand for assistance through Pennsylvania’s EITC and Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit (OSTC) programs. Members also discussed the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit and efforts to urge Gov. Josh Shapiro to opt into the program to expand access to educational scholarships. To date, 30 states have opted in.
Community support also helps veterans find companionship and a sense of belonging. Dean Vanzinardi of Veterans Lake Fishing described how donations from local organizations and businesses allow him to provide fishing outings and equipment for veterans. He urged members to address transportation and accessibility barriers that can prevent veterans from taking part.
The testimony also showed what these services mean to the people who rely on them. Kyle Sentz, a father of three, described how New Hope Ministries helped him navigate life as a single parent, providing groceries, assistance with childcare payments and gasoline, and a place to turn when he felt overwhelmed. Shirley Fortunato shared how her church and the local senior center helped during her recovery from an injury.
Rowe closed the hearing by thanking those who shared their experiences and emphasizing that community generosity must be matched by action in Harrisburg to make everyday necessities more affordable.
“I think today's testimony has really put a human face on a lot of the challenges that Pennsylvania families deal with every day. It's shown the difference that local organizations can make in helping families through difficult times,” Rowe said. “You know, for a family wondering how they'll get through the week, having somewhere to turn in your community really matters.”

title: Rasel, Policy Committee Call for Unleashing Pennsylvania Energy to Lower Costs, Strengthen Reliability
raw_text:
Rasel, Policy Committee Call for Unleashing Pennsylvania Energy to Lower Costs, Strengthen Reliability
September 16, 2026
NORTH HUNTINGDON— Pennsylvania has the resources needed to deliver affordable, reliable energy, but regulatory barriers and misguided policies are preventing the Commonwealth from realizing its full potential, according to testimony presented Monday before the House Republican Policy Committee.
The hearing, titled “Powering Pennsylvania: An Affordable, Reliable Energy Future,” was hosted by Rep. Brian Rasel (R-Westmoreland) and chaired by House Republican Policy Committee Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata).
Testifiers included Matt Mackowiak, director, government affairs, Core Natural Resources; Patrick Henderson, vice president, government affairs and communications, Marcellus Shale Coalition; John Otto, executive director, Citizens Energy Council; and Nick Kerin, deputy state director, Americans for Prosperity – PA.
“While poor policy decisions, some going back many years ago, continue to drive up energy costs, Pennsylvania residents continue to be bogged down with inflated power bills and questions as to whether our energy infrastructure is dependable and capable to meet our future needs,” Rasel said. “Hearings like this are important not only to help legislators craft better policies, but to provide transparency to the public as to the real inflationary costs driven by their own government. Affordable, reliable energy shouldn’t be a question in a resource-rich environment like Pennsylvania.”
Mackowiak testified that Pennsylvania’s declining supply of baseload generation is contributing to rising electricity prices at a time when demand is rapidly increasing. He noted that Pennsylvania is the nation’s third-largest coal producer, yet many of the coal-fired plants that once supplied reliable electricity have been retired and demolished.
“In summary, higher energy demand and lower supply means increases in power prices,” Mackowiak said. “For Pennsylvanians, dramatic increases in power bills means not being able to put gas in the car. It means less money for groceries. It means the choice between heating your home or going without basic medical care.”
“Baseload power must be protected and expanded where possible,” he continued. “We can't afford to continue losing reliable energy sources, and Pennsylvanians can't afford higher electricity prices as a result.”
Henderson highlighted the benefits Pennsylvania consumers have received from the development of the Marcellus Shale. He testified that Pennsylvania has gone from importing 75% of its natural gas to producing nearly 20% of the nation’s supply, helping to reduce natural gas utility supply costs by between 50% and 74% since 2008.
“We need leadership from the governor to build infrastructure, both natural gas pipelines and electric transmission,” Henderson said. “We urge you to say no to new taxes, be it on power generation or energy production. New taxes are simply taxes on consumers.”
Otto outlined the direct benefits energy development provides to communities in Westmoreland County, including more than $24 million in natural gas impact fee revenue distributed to local municipalities since 2011. He said the revenue supports roads, bridges, emergency services, water and sewer systems, parks, and farmland preservation.
“Let's face it, prices are up, people's bills are up. Here's why. Quite simply, demand is growing faster than supply,” Otto said. “And the answer to that problem is sitting right below us.”
Otto also pushed back against the idea that policymakers must choose between developing energy and protecting the environment.
“It seems as though the environmental activists would like us to believe that you have to pick energy or the environment,” Otto said. “And the reality of it is energy and environment can coexist.”
Kerin warned that Pennsylvania is competing with neighboring states for energy development, manufacturing projects, jobs and private investment. He recommended firm permitting deadlines, greater regulatory predictability and policies that allow large energy users to finance generation needed to support their own operations.
“You cannot say Pennsylvania is open for business while making businesses wait indefinitely for the permission to build,” Kerin said.
Kerin also stressed that Pennsylvania must protect its residents from being forced to subsidize costs created by other states within the PJM Interconnection.
“Pennsylvania can be the powerhouse of the Mid-Atlantic. We should not just become its blank check,” Kerin said. “Let's make Pennsylvania the easiest place in PJM to build the next megawatt and the hardest place to stick families with somebody else's bill.”
Rowe said higher energy costs reach far beyond monthly utility bills, raising the cost of food, transportation, manufacturing and nearly every product or service Pennsylvanians purchase.
“We have energy resources to deliver affordability and reliability, but families are still paying higher bills, and warnings about the reliability of our grid continue to grow louder,” Rowe said. “These are the consequences of policies that obstruct production, delay projects, and leave consumers to pay the price.”
“Simply put, enough is enough,” Rowe continued. “It's time to unleash our energy supply, produce more power, and put Pennsylvanians first.”
Rasel concluded that Pennsylvania’s energy policies have real consequences for families struggling to afford basic necessities.
“There's absolutely no reason in Pennsylvania that a widow should have to choose between paying a medical bill or keeping her lights on,” Rasel said. “There's no reason that a mother or a father should have to choose between keeping their home warm or feeding their children.”

Kutz, Policy Committee Highlight Tax Relief Plan to Make Pennsylvania More Affordable
September 3, 2026
MECHANICSBURG
— Rep. Thomas Kutz (R-Cumberland) and the House Republican Policy Committee, led by Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata), convened a hearing Tuesday to examine Kutz’s Growth and Affordability Plan (GAP), a 10-bill package aimed at lowering costs for families and improving Pennsylvania’s economic competitiveness.
The plan includes proposals to reduce Pennsylvania’s Personal Income Tax, lower utility and homeownership costs, make childcare more affordable, help families save for major expenses and improve the Commonwealth’s tax environment for businesses.
“This hearing underscored just how deeply Pennsylvanians care about building a stronger, more affordable future,” said Kutz. “I’m grateful to every colleague, testifier, and community member who engaged with the Growth and Affordability Plan, which I am so proud to sponsor.  Their insights and experiences will shape our legislation, easing costs for families, supporting local employers, and ensuring Pennsylvania remains a place where people want to raise families and build businesses. I remain excited about the work ahead.”
Testifiers included Neal Lesher, vice president of government affairs for the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry; Shelby Linton-Keddie, senior director of government, regulatory policy and external affairs for PPL Electric Utilities; and Matt Madden, operating principal of Keller Williams of Central PA.
Lesher discussed Pennsylvania’s progress in reducing its Corporate Net Income Tax while emphasizing the need for additional reforms to help businesses compete and grow.
“For businesses, cash is like water, right? It’s going to go to the least restrictive place,” Lesher said. “And Pennsylvania, while we’re making improvements, definitely has room for improvement.”
Linton-Keddie testified that eliminating Pennsylvania’s Gross Receipts Tax on electricity, as proposed in the GAP package, would provide direct savings to ratepayers.
“For the average PPL electric residential customer, the savings would be about $12 a month or roughly $150 a year,” Linton-Keddie said. “At a time when many families and businesses are carefully managing household budgets and business budgets to meet their basic expenses, this type of direct, transparent, and permanent tax relief should not be dismissed.”
She stressed that tax relief must be accompanied by policies that increase Pennsylvania’s electricity supply and protect reliability.
“Pennsylvania cannot afford to take potential solutions off the table while affordability and reliability concerns continue to grow,”
Linton-Keddie said. “We believe that our customers deserve affordable, reliable electricity, and that will require a willingness by every one of us to examine every component of the bill and every policy contributing to rising costs.”
Madden described a housing shortage that is limiting options for first-time buyers, renters, growing families and seniors. He urged policymakers to modernize the approval process and encourage the construction of a wider range of housing options.
“Housing supply is a chain, and when one part of the chain stops moving, the effects travel all the way down the market,” Madden said. “Again, housing affordability is a workforce infrastructure just as much as roads, utilities, and broadband are.”
“Affordability is not just about simply what things cost. It’s about how much Pennsylvanians get to keep of their own hard-earned money,” Rowe said. “Every tax the government imposes leaves less for a family’s priorities or business’s next investment. The Growth and Affordability Plan puts that question squarely before us: Where can Harrisburg take less so Pennsylvanians can do more?”

title: Verobish, Policy Committee Highlight Impact of Rising Energy Costs on Pennsylvania Businesses
raw_text:
Verobish, Policy Committee Highlight Impact of Rising Energy Costs on Pennsylvania Businesses
September 2, 2026
ALTOONA
—Rising energy costs are limiting business growth, straining workers, and driving up the price of goods throughout Pennsylvania, employers and industry leaders testified Thursday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing hosted by Rep. Andrea Verobish (R-Blair).
The hearing, “Keeping Pennsylvania Moving: Addressing the Rising Cost of Energy,” was held at Ward Transport and Logistics Corp. in Altoona. Testifiers included Bill Ward Jr., president and CEO of Ward Transport and Logistics; Richard Weyant, facilities maintenance manager at Shirley’s Cookie Company; and Stephanie Catarino Wissman, executive director of API Pennsylvania.
“Pennsylvania has an incredible energy advantage. We have abundant natural resources, a skilled workforce, and along tradition of powering our nation with energy,” Verobish said. “We should ask ourselves why a state with so many energy resources can't do more to ensure affordable, reliable energy for people who live there.”
Verobish has authored a proposal as part of the House Republican “Lights On, Costs Down” energy package, a series of 11 bills intended to increase energy production, improve reliability and lower costs. Her legislation would establish a grid maintenance fee on electricity transported through Pennsylvania to other states and use the revenue to provide reliability credits for electricity consumed within the Commonwealth.
Ward explained that higher energy costs ultimately return to the transportation industry through the rising price of vehicles, equipment, electricity and other necessities.
“Essentially, the tools we need to move America and Pennsylvania forward are becoming more and more expensive,” Ward said. “This reduces our margins and makes it difficult to provide exceptional benefits and pay raises for all employees.”
Ward also described the pressure higher gasoline, heating and consumer prices place on employees. Those financial pressures can lead workers to seek higher wages, change jobs or take second jobs, while employers face significant costs to recruit and train their replacements.
Weyant testified that Shirley’s Cookie Company used less electricity in June 2026 than it did during the same period in 2022, yet its monthly electric bill increased by more than $7,000. That increase came despite the company investing hundreds of thousands of dollars in LED lighting, more efficient HVAC systems and other energy-saving improvements.
“The problem is that the increases in the cost of electricity outweigh any savings we are trying to make from these investments,” Weyant said.
Higher operating costs also leave the company with less money for employee compensation, equipment, automation and expansion. Weyant said Shirley’s currently has approximately $500,000 in automation projects on hold amid uncertainty surrounding electricity and fuel costs.
“We can't just pass every increase on to our customers. We compete with manufacturers from other states and other countries. Our customers have a choice,” Weyant said. “Many of these increases must be absorbed by us as a business.”
Wissman testified that Pennsylvania possesses the resources needed to meet rising demand but needs additional pipelines, power plants, natural gas storage and other infrastructure to deliver that energy reliably and affordably. She also called for more predictable permitting processes, regulatory certainty, and policies protecting consumers’ ability to choose the energy sources that best meet their needs.
“Affordability depends on a reliable energy supply,” Wissman said. “Pennsylvania can't lower costs if we make it harder to produce…the energy on which our economy depends.”
Rep. Josh Kail (R-Beaver/Washington), who spearheaded the package of “Lights On, Costs Down” legislation, emphasized that energy affordability affects the entire economy.
“What we must always remember is that it all comes back to the accessibility of energy, because the lower the cost of energy, the lower the cost of everything else,” Kail said.
Verobish said testimony from the businesses demonstrated how energy expenses ripple throughout Pennsylvania’s economy before ultimately reaching consumers.
“We all face these issues in our personal lives, but hearing businesses explain how these challenges affect our economy and how these prices are passed on to consumers, we are in a vicious circle from which we must escape,” Verobish said. “I am committed to working with my team to make this happen, so we can free up these resources and make Pennsylvania a better place to live, work and develop.”

title: Kozak, Policy Committee Advance Solutions to Keep the Lights On, Costs Down
raw_text:
Kozak, Policy Committee Advance Solutions to Keep the Lights On, Costs Down
August 31, 2026
BEAVER COUNTY—Pennsylvania can lower electricity costs, strengthen grid reliability and attract new investment by expanding energy production, removing regulatory barriers and allowing energy sources to compete in the marketplace, testifiers told lawmakers Wednesday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing.
The hearing, “Keeping the Lights On and Costs Down: Securing Pennsylvania’s Energy Future,” was hosted by Rep. Roman Kozak (R-Beaver) at Bolland Machine in Chippewa Township.
“Natural gas, coal, nuclear—these sources of energy—they are not a problem. They are a blessing,” Kozak said. “They are an amazing thing that helps us run our economy. They help us be the greatest country in the world.”
Kozak said government mandates that favor certain energy sources have increased costs without adequately addressing Pennsylvania’s need for dependable baseload power. The Commonwealth’s Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards Act requires electric utilities to obtain a portion of their electricity from government-designated sources. Kozak is proposing to replace the law with an Affordable Energy Portfolio Standards Act as part of the House Republican “Lights On, Costs Down” energy package.
“My legislation would refocus Pennsylvania’s energy policy on what matters most to consumers, dependable power, predictable markets and lower energy bills,” Kozak said. “It's really simple. Energy sources should compete based on their ability and affordability and their reliability in our homes and in our businesses, not because one technology has been favored by the government.”
Testifiers included Kevin Bolland, sales manager and vice president of operations at Bolland Machine; Emily Stipe, director of federal and political affairs at Vistra Corp.; Kevin Hennessy, senior director of policy at Mainspring Energy; and Laura DelVecchio, administrative director of the Beaver County Career and Technology Center.
Bolland described how energy and infrastructure costs affect his family-owned company, which has operated in Beaver County since 1962 and provides machining and repair services for natural gas engines and compressors.
“Energy isn't just an overhead for us, it's a raw material,” Bolland said.
He explained that the company recently considered adding the electrical capacity needed to operate new machinery but received a quote exceeding $100,000. The business instead reconfigured its equipment to operate on less-efficient power.
“That utility barrier forces us to run less efficient every single day,” Bolland said.
Stipe said Pennsylvania possesses abundant natural gas, an existing nuclear fleet, a skilled workforce and a competitive electricity market capable of attracting private investment. However, developers need greater certainty before committing to projects that can take decades to develop and operate.
“The most important thing the government can provide industry to enable the building of additional energy infrastructure is certainty,” Stipe said. “That includes permit certainty, whether you're a natural gas pipeline or a solar or wind farm, knowing that if your project has all of its requisite permits, they will not suddenly be revoked when there is a change in administration or political power.”
Stipe also emphasized the importance of preserving existing generation while new energy resources are developed.
“Keeping in mind both affordability and reliability needs, the quickest and cheapest megawatt is the one already connected to the grid,” she said.
Hennessy discussed Mainspring Energy’s plans to establish a manufacturing center in the Pittsburgh region that is expected to employ approximately 120 skilled workers during its initial phase. He said the company’s flexible power-generation technology should be permitted to compete on equal footing with other energy sources.
“Our request is to be part of the dialogue, to be part of the conversation,” Hennessy said. “We've got a great technology that's a really good fit for Pennsylvania.
DelVecchio said Pennsylvania must also strengthen its career and technical education system to prepare the workers needed by the energy and manufacturing industries. Sixteen of the Beaver County Career and Technology Center’s 17 programs are currently at capacity, leaving some students unable to pursue their preferred career path.
“Pennsylvania has an opportunity to build its energy and workforce by investing in students that are already here,” DelVecchio said. “The students, not only at the Beaver County Career and Technology Center, but Western Pennsylvania shouldn't have to leave here to go elsewhere to find those life-sustaining wages.”
Policy Committee Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata) said Pennsylvania must capitalize on its resources, workforce and expertise to meet rising demand while protecting families and businesses from higher costs.
“If we fail to act, Pennsylvania's family and businesses will continue paying more for a grid that becomes less reliable,” Rowe said. “Pennsylvania should not be managing energy scarcity. We should be leading the nation in energy production.”
Also participating in the hearing were Reps. Josh Kail (R-Beaver/Washington), Jake Banta (R-Erie), Brian Rasel (R-Westmoreland), Jeremy Shaffer (R-Allegheny), Parke Wentling (R-Mercer) and Eric Nelson (R-Westmoreland).

raw_text:
Weaknecht, Policy Committee Highlight Solutions to Strengthen Law Enforcement Workforce
August 20, 2026
BERKS COUNTY
— Pennsylvania can address its law enforcement staffing shortage without lowering professional standards by strengthening career pipelines; improving training; and supporting the physical, mental and financial well-being of officers, according to law enforcement leaders who testified Wednesday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing.
The hearing, “Protecting Pennsylvania: Law Enforcement Recruitment and Retention,” was hosted by Rep. Eric Weaknecht (R-Berks) at Reading Regional Airport. Testifiers included Bern Township Police Chief Brett Forry; Carbon County Sheriff Daniel Zeigler,
representing the Pennsylvania Sheriffs’ Association; Pennsylvania State Police (PSP) Lt. Col. Christopher King and Special Assistant Brooke Meade; and Greg Rowe, senior counsel to Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday.
Also participating were Policy Committee Vice Chair Kristin Marcell (R-Bucks), Reps. Dan Moul (R-Adams), Mark Gillen (R-Berks), and David Zimmerman (R-Lancaster/Berks), along with representatives from the offices of U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick and Congressman Dan Meuser.
“Recruiting law enforcement officers is critical to keeping our communities safe,” said Weaknecht. “As sheriff, one of my greatest challenges was training qualified deputies only to lose them to departments that could offer higher pay or better benefits. Now, as a state representative, I want to ensure those on the front lines have a voice in identifying what the Commonwealth can do to help.”
Pennsylvania employed approximately 24,300 police officers and sheriff’s deputies in 2024—an 11-year low and a 14% decline since 2013. Testifiers said departments that once received hundreds of applications for a single opening may now receive only a handful, while agencies compete against one another and the private sector for qualified candidates.
“Pennsylvania does not need to lower its standards to address this workforce challenge,” said Rowe. “We need to strengthen the pipeline into law enforcement, support those who serve, and restore the respect that will encourage qualified young people to view law enforcement as a meaningful, family-sustaining career. If we want talented people to enter the profession and experienced officers to remain, we must demonstrate through both our words and our policies that their service matters.”
Forry said the staffing crisis is already increasing overtime, fatigue and stress among officers. He recommended tuition assistance, academy scholarships, student loan repayment, recruitment incentives, and additional state support for training and officer wellness.
“Officer wellness is no longer optional; it is essential,” he testified. “Healthy officers provide better service to our communities.”
Zeigler described significant disparities in pay and benefits among counties. He said deputies may complete 19 weeks of academy training only to leave for a neighboring county offering substantially higher compensation for the same work. His office is currently operating at half staffing while remaining responsible for court security, prisoner transportation, warrant service, and other duties.
Greg Rowe emphasized that retention is especially important as criminal investigations become increasingly complex. “Experience matters,” he testified, pointing to sophisticated drug and human trafficking operations, technology-enabled crimes, and cases involving traumatized victims.”
King reported that the Pennsylvania State Police currently has 210 trooper vacancies and said the statutory complement cap limits the agency’s ability to train cadets in anticipation of future retirements. He encouraged lawmakers to remove the cap, an approach that has previously received bipartisan support in the General Assembly.
“We anticipate having a large number of retirements at the beginning of next year, and we cannot fill those positions fast enough,” King said. “Removing the complement cap would help us anticipate those workforce needs and give us greater flexibility to meet them.”
Testifiers also highlighted the importance of reaching prospective officers earlier through high school, technical education, college, youth leadership, and mentorship programs. They stressed that compensation alone will not solve the problem.

title: Gaydos, Mihalek, Shaffer and Policy Committee Highlight Need for Accountability in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing
raw_text:
Gaydos, Mihalek, Shaffer and Policy Committee Highlight Need for Accountability in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing
August 14, 2026
ALLEGHENY COUNTY
—Pennsylvania’s lack of a clear sentencing framework for second-degree murder could produce inconsistent sentences, overwhelm courts and force victims’ families to repeatedly relive the murders of their loved ones, prosecutors testified Thursday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing.
The hearing, “Protecting Pennsylvania: Accountability and Justice in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing,” was hosted by Reps. Valerie Gaydos (R-Moon Township), Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny) and Jeremy Shaffer (R-Allegheny) at the Moon Township Municipal Building.
In March, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that automatically imposing life without parole in every second-degree murder case, without considering an offender’s individual role and level of responsibility, violates the Pennsylvania Constitution. The court gave the General Assembly 120 days to establish a new sentencing framework, but the deadline passed without a final measure reaching the governor’s desk.
“No court ruling or legislative action can undo the loss these families have endured, but we can ensure their voices are heard and respected as Pennsylvania determines its path forward,” said House Republican Policy Committee Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata). “Victims’ families deserve more than uncertainty. They deserve meaningful participation in the process and confidence that the justice system will never forget the life that was taken.”
Rowe opened the hearing by reading letters submitted by Stella Getgen and Christine Hickman, the wife and sister of murder victim Todd Getgen. Both described the loss their family has endured since his 2010 murder and the renewed trauma caused by the possibility that his killer’s sentence could be reconsidered.
Todd Getgen’s son was 6 years old when his father was murdered and has grown up without him. In her letter, Stella Getgen described having to explain to her young son why his father would never return, while assuring him that the man responsible would remain in prison. Hickman wrote that while her brother’s killer received life, Todd “didn’t get life; he got death.”
“Pennsylvania must get second-degree murder sentencing right—for victims, families and public safety,” said Gaydos. “Law enforcement has made clear how serious this issue is, yet without a consistent sentencing framework, our judicial system is in chaos and public safety is in jeopardy. Pennsylvanians should be outraged that House Philadelphia Democrats chose politics over public safety. It’s time to restore the rule of law, hold violent offenders accountable and demand that House Democrats take up this legislation immediately.”
Testimony was provided by Ronald M. Wabby Jr., deputy district attorney for the Critical Case Review Unit, Appellate Division, Allegheny County District Attorney’s Office; Westmoreland County District Attorney Nicole Ziccarelli; and Indiana County District Attorney Robert Manzi.
Wabby said Allegheny County has more than 160 individuals convicted of second-degree murder in cases dating to the 1970s. Drawing on his experience with juvenile-lifer resentencings, he warned that without a statewide framework, inconsistent sentences and years of additional appeals could force victims’ families to repeatedly revisit murders committed decades earlier.
“There is no finality that I can give a victim,” Wabby testified. “When a victim is forced to relive events decades later, I can’t explain to you the pain I saw in these people’s eyes.”
Mihalek, a former Allegheny County prosecutor, criticized House leaders for allowing partisan politics to derail a bipartisan sentencing solution, stressing that accountability for violent offenders is fundamental to public safety.
"In a day and age when the average Pennsylvania resident is done with partisan nonsense, House leaders played a dangerous game by waiting until the final hours of the court's deadline to amend a commonsense bill first passed by the Senate," Mihalek said. "Holding accountable violent criminals, convicted of some of the most atrocious crimes possible against their fellow man, is not a political game – it's a cornerstone of public safety. I'm happy to discuss prison reforms for nonviolent offenders and offering hands up to help them change their lives, but I am completely opposed to simply unlocking the cell doors for Pennsylvania's most violent criminals."
Ziccarelli testified that approximately 1,100 people currently serving second-degree murder sentences could seek resentencing or possible release. She said the resulting proceedings would impose significant costs on taxpayers, strain courts and prosecutors, and jeopardize public safety.
She recommended preserving victims’ statutory rights to participate in parole proceedings, protecting the finality of plea agreements and establishing a mandatory minimum sentence while retaining life without parole for the most serious cases.
Ziccarelli also discussed a pending Westmoreland County case involving the murder of Anthony Williams, a 31-year-old father of five. His family waited five years for a jury verdict but continues to await a final sentence because no legislative framework is in place.
Manzi rejected portrayals of second-degree murder defendants as innocent bystanders. He explained that a conviction requires participation as a principal or accomplice in an underlying felony such as robbery, rape, arson, burglary or kidnapping, during which a death occurs. He then detailed several Indiana County cases involving shootings, beatings and other brutal murders.
Shaffer said testimony from law enforcement underscored the seriousness of the issue and the need for a statewide solution that protects victims’ families and ensures uniform justice.
“I’ve expressed my disappointment regarding the situation surrounding second-degree murder sentencing. It was good to hear from law enforcement officials about the seriousness of this issue. We need to move forward with a solution to protect victims’ families and have uniform justice across the state,” said Shaffer.
The prosecutors expressed support for key elements of
Senate Bill 1400
, which would establish a minimum sentence of 35 years with a maximum of life imprisonment, preserve life without parole under specified circumstances, and create a structured parole process for certain people already serving second-degree murder sentences.
House Democrats amended
House Bill 1042
to remove the Senate’s bipartisan sentencing framework and add unrelated medical parole and other provisions. Those changes prevented the legislation from receiving final approval before the court’s deadline and perpetuated the legal uncertainty facing prosecutors, courts and victims’ families.
Written testimony was also submitted by John Rago, a Duquesne University Kline School of Law professor, Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing member, and chairman of the Center for Victims board; the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association; and Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 91.
The House Republican Policy Committee will continue examining second-degree murder sentencing at another public hearing in the coming weeks.
